All solid wastes would either be incinerated or collected by privately contracted waste handlers. Applicable regulations would be followed in handling all solid wastes.
3.2.5.2 Domestic Wastes
Domestic wastes from the powerhouse during operation would be handled by either a septic tank system or a permanent waste treatment plant. Soil tests would be conducted to determine which type of facility to use.
3.2.6 Use of Resources
Since the proposed project would pump water from the existing Jocassee Lake and return it, the only commitment of the Jocassee water resource by the project would be the loss due to evaporation from the upper reservoir and dead storage. The drainage area of the upper reservoir is only 1.5 square miles and the natural runoff would be mixed with pumped water from Lake Jocassee within the upper reservoir.
About 820 acres of land would be disrupted due to the construction of the project, including the transmission line corridor. Clearing required for road, switchyard, and transmission line corridor would necessitate removal of vegetation.
The pump-back operation to the upper reservoir would require energy from other resources. It would take about 4 kWh of pumping to produce 3 kWh of generation. The upper reservoir would have a storage capacity which could produce 32,000 MWh of energy. The pumping energy would come from the Applicant's Oconee Nuclear Plant.
Operation of the Bad Creek Project would require the annual use of an estimated 1,200 pounds of industrial grease, 100 to 300 gallons of governor oil, 50 gallons of commercial solvent, and 0.7 tons of incremental nuclear fuel (at a base load nuclear powerplant).
